name: Back Hall
description: The second circulation system. A back hall exists so that one set of people can move through the house without meeting another set, and everything about it - its position, its width, its finish, its lack of daylight - follows from the fact that it was designed to be invisible from the formal plan. It is one of only two rooms in the domestic catalogue that were built specifically to enforce a social separation, the other being the centre passage, and it is the one whose original population has entirely gone and been replaced by a different one.

history.replaced_by: the mudroom, which is the same room serving children, dogs and shopping instead of servants
history.note: THE BACK HALL IS ABOUT PEOPLE, NOT ABOUT LUGGAGE. Its rise tracks the rise of the live-in servant almost exactly: it appears in English planning in the 1690s, becomes standard in any house with more than two servants through the eighteenth century, and reaches its most elaborate form in the 1880s, when a large house might have four separate circulation systems - family, guests, servants and tradesmen - that never intersect. The point was never efficiency. It was that a servant carrying a chamber pot at seven in the morning must not be met on the stairs. Then the servant supply collapses - in Britain between 1914 and 1939, in America a generation earlier as immigration patterns and factory wages changed - and the back hall loses its whole population within about twenty years. It survives in plan as the route from the kitchen to the back door, and it comes back with a new name and a new population around 1990, when the garage-to-kitchen route needs somewhere to put boots. The mechanism is worth stating: the plan element outlived the social structure that produced it, was carried forward as a habit, and was then reoccupied.

dimensions.critical_dimension: WIDTH, and the honest number is 42 in rather than 36, because this is the corridor that carries LOADS: a laundry basket is 26 in wide and is carried on the hip, a tray is 24 in, a vacuum cleaner and its operator take 30 in. Every one of those makes a 36 in corridor a single-file corridor with no room to pass. The second dimension is the BACK STAIR, and here the geometry is genuinely different from the principal stair: a service stair at 36 in wide with a 7.75 in rise and a winder turn was normal and is now largely illegal, so a modern back stair takes as much plan as a front one and there is no longer any dimensional saving in having two. That single change in the code is a large part of why the second stair disappeared from ordinary houses.

furniture.note: 18 in of bench plus 36 in to sit and pull a boot off is 54 in of depth; a 42 in corridor cannot have a bench in it and a mudroom is therefore a different room, not a wide back hall

daylight.orientation: North or whatever is left. The back hall historically took the elevation nobody looked at, which is exactly why it should get the one window it can have: a borrowed light or a glazed back door at the end of the run.
daylight.note: This is the second-rank borrowed-light room from the room-vernacular pack, at 1.2 times head height rather than 2.25, and it is the clearest case in the catalogue of the daylight rule assigning a room its function rather than the other way round. Put a room 20 ft back from the only window wall in a double-pile plan and it is a service room whether you intended it or not - no quantity of downlights changes what it feels like to be in. The one move that works is a glazed back door on the axis, which lights the corridor its full length for the price of a door.

must_adjoin.why: the back hall's entire reason for existing is to connect the kitchen to the rest of the house and to the outside without crossing the formal plan

should_adjoin.why: in the modern plan they are consecutive: garage, mudroom, back hall, kitchen, and the sequence is the same one the tradesman's entrance had
laundry is the heaviest and wettest traffic in the house and belongs on the service route, not on the family corridor
the pantry is the dining room's end of the same service route the back hall is the kitchen's end of
a WC on the back hall serves the garden, the garage and the kitchen without putting a WC door on the entrance hall

must_not_adjoin.why: if the back hall opens onto the front hall then the two circulation systems have merged and the house has paid for both and got one. They may LAND on the same upper corridor at opposite ends, which is different.
exceptions: small plans under about 1,800 sq ft, where a single circulation spine is the honest answer and pretending otherwise produces two bad corridors instead of one good one

must_not_adjoin.why: the back hall is the unfinished side of the house and a door from it into the dining room delivers noise and view; the butler's pantry exists precisely to be the airlock at this junction

servicing.ventilation: This is where the house's wet traffic runs, and a back hall with no extract and a door to the laundry is where the humidity load ends up. One 50 cfm extract, or a window.
servicing.heat: Minimal, but not none: an unheated back hall against a heated kitchen is where condensation collects on the coldest surface in the house.
servicing.electrical: Switched at both ends and at the door to the garage. This is the corridor people walk in the dark with their hands full.

style_variation.note: Fully developed: a service corridor in the basement or in a wing, a back stair rising the full height, and the whole system detailed in a deliberately different and plainer trim family from the state rooms - stone flags rather than boards, painted deal rather than mahogany, no cornice. The trim grade IS the signal, and using one trim grade for the whole house destroys it.

The 1880s American house at its most elaborate carries a back stair from kitchen to servants' rooms in the attic, bypassing the family floor entirely - four storeys of circulation that no member of the family ever used.
Kept as a habit after the servants were gone, which is why so many 1920s Colonial Revival houses have a narrow back stair whose original purpose the owners cannot explain.

Fully revived and now the house's real front door, since the family arrives by car. The interesting inversion is that it is now finished BETTER than the formal hall in many plans - shiplap, lockers, a bench, a feature light - because it is the one everyone uses.

Single storey and no servants: the type collapses the whole service route into a door between the carport and the kitchen. This is honest and is one of the reasons the ranch plan works better than its reputation.
No second circulation of any kind. The house is one route.

The service route is OUTSIDE: the kitchen is a detached kitchen house in the yard and the connection is across open ground or along the piazza's rear end. Fire, heat and smell all argued for detachment in a subtropical climate, and the back hall as an interior room barely exists in the type.

code.requirement: Hallways not less than 36 in; a second stairway must meet the same rise, run, headroom and handrail requirements as the first.
code.conflict: This is the rule that killed the back stair. The historic service stair was steep, narrow and winder-turned, and made its case by taking half the plan area of the principal stair. Made to modern geometry it takes the same area, so the second stair now costs a full room's worth of floor on two storeys - about 90 sq ft - and is cut from the drawing on the first cost review.

code.requirement: A door between the garage and the dwelling must be a solid wood or solid or honeycomb core steel door not less than 1 3/8 in thick, or a 20-minute fire-rated door, self-closing.
code.conflict: The self-closer is routinely removed by the occupants within a month and is the most-defeated safety device in the house. Detail the opening so the door can be handsome and heavy enough that the closer is not resented.

sources: Robert Kerr, The Gentleman's House (1864), on the separation of family and service circulation
Mark Girouard, Life in the English Country House (1978), chapter 9
